drug_class: Selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE compound) / anticancer agent
purpose: Selinexor is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of multiple myeloma (a cancer of the blood) and a type of lymphoma called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). It is usually used when other treatments have stopped working or are no longer an option. Your doctor may use it alone or combined with other cancer medicines.
how_it_works: Inside your cells, there is a protein called XPO1 that acts like a doorway, letting certain protective proteins escape from the cell's control center (the nucleus). Cancer cells take advantage of this to keep growing. Selinexor blocks that doorway, keeping those protective proteins inside the nucleus where they can stop cancer cells from growing and cause them to die. Healthy cells are much less affected by this process.
common_side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (very common), decreased appetite and weight loss, tiredness and weakness, diarrhea, low blood cell counts (which can cause increased risk of infection, bruising, or bleeding), low sodium levels in the blood, confusion or memory problems, and dizziness. Your care team will monitor you closely for these.
warnings: Selinexor can cause seriously low blood counts, which raises your risk of dangerous infections and bleeding — call your doctor right away if you have a fever, unusual bruising, or signs of infection. It can cause dangerously low sodium levels in the blood, which may lead to confusion, seizures, or falls. It may cause neurological problems like confusion or balance issues, so be careful driving or operating machinery. It can harm an unborn baby, so both men and women must use reliable birth control during and after treatment. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, as interactions are possible.
typical_dosing: The most common dose is 80 mg taken by mouth once a week, on the same day each week, in combination with other medicines — but your doctor may adjust this based on your specific condition and how well you tolerate it. Take it with food and a full glass of water to help reduce nausea. Do not crush or split the tablets. If you miss a dose, do not double up — just ask your care team what to do.
